claims.text: High configurational disorder produces uneven atomic bonding and increased lattice friction.
Local lattice distortions generate heterogeneous barriers to dislocation motion.
Local lattice distortions impede uniform dislocation motion in high-entropy alloys.
Uneven bonding and lattice friction create localized stress concentrations during rapid deformation.
The heterogeneous barriers and localized stresses promote activation of secondary slip systems.
The heterogeneous barriers and localized stresses promote deformation twinning or nanotwinning.
Activation of secondary slip and twinning retards strain localization.
Secondary slip and twinning jointly enhance strength and ductility during high-strain-rate deformation.
Under dynamic loading, high-entropy alloys will have a higher strain-hardening rate than conventional single-principal-element alloys of similar crystal structure.
Under dynamic loading, high-entropy alloys will exhibit delayed necking relative to the conventional-alloy baseline.
Under dynamic loading, high-entropy alloys will exhibit more twinning than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Under dynamic loading, high-entropy alloys will exhibit greater activation of secondary slip than the conventional-alloy baseline.
High-entropy alloys will exhibit higher dynamic strength than the conventional-alloy baseline.
High-entropy alloys will exhibit greater dynamic ductility than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Conventional single-principal-element alloys generally exhibit more homogeneous dislocation motion than high-entropy alloys.
Conventional single-principal-element alloys generally exhibit less pronounced secondary deformation mechanisms than high-entropy alloys.
At extremely high temperatures, recovery or recrystallization may alter the proposed deformation mechanism.
Under quasi-static loading, the operative deformation mechanism may differ from the proposed dynamic mechanism.
